name: Maya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small studio of four in a converted barn just outside town. Our biggest client is the farmers' co-op, so I do their price lists, feed bag labels and the monthly newsletter. We also do the bakery chain's posters, church fête flyers and quite a lot of wedding stationery. Today I'm finishing the co-op's spring catalogue, which is mostly photos of seed drills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, and I like that my work ends up in the hands of farmers I've met. What wears me out is the low pay and the long drive in the winter. My partner Daniel works at the hardware store, and between us we've got about three weeks of money spare. We want to get married and start a family, so that number bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, good honest work still matters. I'd say it at church and to the girls I went to college with. I'd also admit I use it a bit, for first drafts of the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's okay, but the money isn't. The co-op has said they might print fewer catalogues next year. And Daniel and I can't save for a wedding on what we earn now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool for newsletter drafts, since it saves me an hour a week. I'd ask Clive (who owns the studio) for more wedding stationery work, because that pays better per hour. And I'd set aside fifty a month in a wedding pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's fine, but we feel stuck on the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being stuck look like in a year's time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still renting the little flat above the launderette, still saying next year for the wedding. Daniel would be fine with it, he's patient. I'm the one who'd mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the wedding matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I was raised, you marry and then you start a family. My mum and dad married with no money and they managed. I'd like to do it properly, though, not on a credit card.

say: I'd say **good honest work** still matters, at church and to college friends.
I'd admit I use AI a bit for the co-op's **newsletter drafts**.
think: My job's okay, but the **money** isn't enough to save for a wedding.
The co-op may print **fewer catalogues** next year, which means less work.
do: Keep using AI for drafts, saving **an hour a week**.
Ask Clive (the owner) for more **wedding stationery** work.
Put **fifty a month** into a wedding pot.
S0.quote: My mum and dad married with no money and they managed. I'd like to do it properly, though, not on a credit card.
fieldNote: Maya's worry is **saving for a wedding**, not AI.
She uses AI **casually** and admits it openly.
Her values centre on **marriage and family**, which drive her money plans.

steps.text: Ask Clive for more wedding stationery work
Use AI for first drafts of the co-op newsletter
Put fifty a month into a wedding savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, but people adapt, they always have. I'd tell younger ones to learn a trade alongside design. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the co-op will do their own newsletters and price lists with AI. That's half my work. Clive would keep me on for a while, but there'd be fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the newer tools properly once I see other studios using them, so I'm the one who sets it up for the co-op. I'd ask my mum about dental nursing, because her practice trains people on the job. And Daniel and I would put the wedding back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see half my week disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mum's done it twenty years and loves it. You're with people, your hands are busy, and there's an apprenticeship so you earn while you learn. It's not glamorous but it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car is the big one. I'd look for a cheaper one or share Daniel's. And no holiday this year, we'd stay home.

say: I'd say it's a big change, but people **adapt**, they always have.
I'd tell younger designers to learn **a trade** alongside design.
think: The co-op will do its own **newsletters** and price lists.
That's **half my work**, and my hours would drop.
do: Ask Mum about a **dental nursing** apprenticeship.
S1.quote: The co-op will do their own newsletters and price lists with AI. That's half my work.
fieldNote: Maya's biggest client is the one most likely to **do it themselves**.
Her fallback is a **dental nursing apprenticeship**, following her mother.
The **wedding** is the first thing she'd delay.

steps.text: Set up AI tools for the co-op's newsletter before they go elsewhere
Ask Mum's dental practice about a nursing apprenticeship
Put the wedding back a year
Swap the car for a cheaper one or share Daniel's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and families need to pull together. I'd want the government to back apprenticeships, not just hand out money. I'd vote for whoever says that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my design job's gone within a year. It's all screen work, so it goes on the AGI date. Daniel's job at the hardware store is hands-on, so he probably has until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the dental nursing apprenticeship as soon as Mum's practice would take me. We'd marry small, at the registry office, and save the church for later. I'd sell the car and get a lift with Mum to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Everything I planned would move at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doesn't AGI touch dental work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking and the notes, yes, on the first date. But someone has to hold the suction and calm the child who's crying at the dentist. That bit waits for the robots, about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be thrilled I was following her. Dad would worry about the money. Daniel's parents would tell us to move in with them, and we might.

say: I'd say it's frightening and families need to **pull together**.
I'd vote for whoever backs **apprenticeships** rather than just handing out money.
think: My **design job** goes within a year, because it's all screen work.
Daniel's **hands-on** job at the hardware store probably lasts until 2031.
do: Sell the car and get **lifts** with Mum.
feel: **Alarmed**, with everything she planned **moving at once**.
S2.quote: Someone has to hold the suction and calm the child who's crying at the dentist.
fieldNote: Maya reads the **robot gap** clearly for her new job.
She'd marry at the **registry office** first, church later.
She'd vote for **apprenticeship** backing, not cash support.

steps.text: Start a dental nursing apprenticeship at Mum's practice
Marry at the registry office and save the church wedding for later
Sell the car and ride in with Mum
Vote for the party that funds apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so let's not panic. Families and firms should plan together. That's my honest public view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep designing for two or three more years and then switch. That's enough to get married properly first. It's not ideal, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short evening course on dental nursing, to see if I like it. I'd keep the studio job and save seventy a month. Daniel and I would set the wedding date for summer 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd switch in two or three years. What would make you go earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Clive cut my hours. Or if the co-op dropped us. Then I'd go straight to the apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the wedding, around twenty-nine or thirty. I'd want to be in the new job first, so I'm not starting over pregnant.

say: I'd say five years is time to **prepare**, so let's not panic.
think: I'd keep designing for **two or three** more years, then switch jobs.
That's enough time to **marry properly** first, which matters to me.
do: Take a short **evening course** in dental nursing.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way she **can carry**.
S3.quote: I'd want to be in the new job first, so I'm not starting over pregnant.
fieldNote: Five years lets Maya keep the **wedding** on track.
She'd **test** dental nursing first, true to her steady nature.
She ties her career switch to **having children**.

steps.text: Take an evening course in dental nursing
Save seventy a month from the studio wage
Set the wedding date for summer 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of warning, so everyone should get on with it. Learn a trade, save, look after your family. I'd say it without any fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel fine for now. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. I could marry, have a baby, and then train for something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd learn the AI tools well for the co-op, since that keeps me useful. I'd save for the wedding and marry in 2027. Dental nursing would wait until the kids are a bit older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there in the back of my mind, but it doesn't stop me planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're waiting on retraining. Is there a risk in that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if everyone has the same idea at the same time. I'd keep in touch with Mum's practice so I'm known there. That's how jobs work round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work, in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and something with people. Kindness won't be automated. I'd want them near family, too.

say: I'd say ten years is a **fair warning**, so get on with it.
Learn a trade, **save**, and look after your family.
think: Ten years makes me feel **fine for now**, since I'd be thirty-seven.
I could marry, have a **baby**, and then retrain for something new.
do: Learn the **AI tools** well for the co-op.
S4.quote: Learn something with your hands and something with people. Kindness won't be automated.
fieldNote: With a decade, Maya puts **family first** and career change second.
She relies on **local connections** to get the retraining spot later.
Her advice to future children stresses **hands, people** and kindness.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools well for the co-op's work
Save for the wedding this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everything we planned would have to move at once. What would help is apprenticeships with real wages for people changing jobs, so I could train without us going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family. Every answer I gave was about my partner Daniel and the wedding and kids. I think that's true for most people my age, not just me.

headlineQuote: Every answer I gave was about my partner Daniel and the wedding and kids.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old designer** at a studio whose main client is the **farmers' co-op**.
She uses AI **now and then** and would learn more once it's proven.
Her plans revolve around **marrying Daniel** and starting a family.
Her fallback is a **dental nursing** apprenticeship at her mum's practice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because all her plans would move at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** with **real wages** for people changing jobs.
